examples: Plain 반말 친절해; drop 요 with close friends.
The staff here is really kind.
-들이 marks plural staff; 친절하다 describes how they treat customers.
길을 몰랐는데 어떤 분이 친절하게 가르쳐 주셨어요.
I didn't know the way, but someone kindly showed me.
친절하게 (adverb) + 주시다 honorific = a kind favor done for you.
nuance: 친절하다 is 'kind' in the sense of warm, attentive, service-minded behavior toward others — the word you reach for about staff, neighbors, or strangers who go out of their way for you. It is Sino-Korean 親切 (친 'close/intimate' + 절 'earnest/keen'), literally 'intimately earnest'. Compare 착하다, which is about an inherently good, gentle heart (a moral quality), whereas 친절하다 is about outward considerate treatment in a given moment — a cold person can still be 친절한 at work. It also differs from 다정하다 (affectionate, emotionally close). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation, so 하다 becomes 해요 (친절해요), and the adverb 친절하게 ('kindly') pairs naturally with verbs like 가르쳐 주다 or 설명하다. The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 친절하요 (the 하 must fuse to 해), and don't use it for an object or food — 'kind' as in 'a kind gesture' is fine, but you can't call coffee 친절한.

Treating it like a verb and saying 친절했다 to mean 'acted kindly once' while expecting a do-form — it is an adjective, so to say someone 'was kind to me' you often add the action: 친절하게 대해 줬어요.

examples: 반말 똑똑해; 똑똑하다 works for clever animals too.
That student was smart from a young age.
If you act smart(ly), you won't lose out.
nuance: 똑똑하다 is native Korean (not Sino-Korean), and it means 'smart' in the everyday sense of being quick, sharp, and able to understand and judge well — equally natural for a bright child, a clever student, or a clever pet. The nearest rivals are 영리하다 (clever/shrewd, slightly more about cunning and cute cleverness, often for kids and animals) and 똑똑하다's bookish cousin 지능이 높다 ('high IQ'); 똑똑하다 is the warm spoken word, while 우수하다 (excellent) or 유능하다 (competent/capable) describe proven performance and ability at work rather than raw brains. The adverb 똑똑하게 can drift toward 'shrewdly, without being fooled', as in 똑똑하게 소비하다 ('shop smart'). It takes the regular 하다 conjugation (똑똑해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'smart' in English also means stylish/well-dressed, but 똑똑하다 NEVER means fashionable — for that you need 멋있다 or 옷을 잘 입다 — and beginners often misfire by saying 똑똑하요 instead of the contracted 똑똑해요.

examples: 반말 게을러; 르 irregular gives 게을러.
동생이 너무 게을러서 방 청소를 안 해요.
My sibling is so lazy that they don't clean their room.
요즘 좀 게을러져서 운동을 못 했어요.
I've gotten a bit lazy lately so I couldn't work out.
nuance: 게으르다 means 'lazy/idle', describing someone who avoids effort and puts things off; it is native Korean (not Sino-Korean) and carries a clearly negative, faintly scolding tone, so it is something you say about yourself jokingly or about a close family member, but rarely to a senior's face. Its mirror opposite is 부지런하다 (diligent), and its near-neighbor 느리다 means 'slow' (about speed), which is different — a fast worker can still be 게으른 if they dodge work, and a 게으른 person isn't necessarily 느린. Conjugation is the key lesson: 게으르다 is a 르-irregular verb, so before 어요 the 르 doubles the ㄹ and the vowel becomes 어 → 게을러요 (the stem 게으르- → 게을러-); but the modifier and dictionary-style forms stay regular (게으른 사람, 게으릅니다). Watch the set noun phrase 게으름을 피우다 ('to slack off'). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating it like a regular ㅡ-vowel verb and saying 게으러요 — you must apply the 르 rule to get 게을러요.

Using 게으르다 bluntly about a boss or elder. It is judgmental; soften with humor about yourself (저 오늘 좀 게을렀어요) rather than labeling a superior.

examples: 반말 부지런해; about a hardworking habit.
Diligent people get up early in the morning.
그 친구는 부지런히 공부해서 시험에 붙었어요.
That friend studied diligently and passed the exam.
nuance: 부지런하다 means 'diligent, industrious, hardworking by habit', the warm-praise opposite of 게으르다. The 부지런 part is native Korean (not a hanja compound), joined to 하다. The dividing line with near-synonyms matters: 성실하다 (Sino 誠實, 'sincere/faithful') praises a conscientious, reliable, earnest character — about attitude and trustworthiness — while 부지런하다 emphasizes physically keeping busy, not being idle, getting up early and getting things done; 열심히 하다 ('do hard') describes effort on a specific task in the moment, whereas 부지런하다 is a standing trait. The adverb is irregular in spelling — 부지런히 (not 부지런하게 in everyday use) — as in 부지런히 일하다. It conjugates regularly as a 하다 adjective (부지런해요). The English-speaker pitfall: 'diligent' in English often modifies effort on one job, so learners try to plug 부지런하다 into a single action ('I studied diligently') as a verb; for that, use the adverb 부지런히 + verb, and avoid the beginner error 부지런하요 (it must contract to 부지런해요).

Equating it exactly with 성실하다. 부지런하다 = actively busy/not idle; 성실하다 = sincere and reliable in attitude. For 'a faithful, conscientious worker' 성실하다 fits better than 부지런하다.

usage: adverb 솔직히 as a discourse opener
examples: Honestly, I didn't really like that.
그 친구는 너무 솔직해서 가끔 상처를 줘요.
That friend is so frank that they sometimes hurt people.
솔직해서 (하다 + 서) shows the blunt-honesty edge.
Thank you for the honest feedback.
Modifier 솔직한 + 피드백; common at work.
nuance: 솔직하다 means 'honest, frank, candid' — speaking your real thoughts and feelings openly without hiding or sugar-coating. It is Sino-Korean 率直 (솔/率 'frank, straightforward' + 직/直 'straight'), literally 'frank and straight'. The crucial contrast is with 정직하다 (Sino 正直 'upright-straight'), which is moral honesty — not lying, not cheating, being truthful as an ethical quality; 솔직하다 is about emotional candor, saying what you really feel, even bluntly, so 솔직하다 can sometimes mean 'too blunt', while 정직하다 is unambiguously praise. The adverb 솔직히 ('honestly, to be frank') is one of the most common conversation openers in Korean (솔직히 말하면…). It follows the regular 하다 conjugation (솔직해요). English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 솔직하다 when you mean morally honest/trustworthy (use 정직하다), and never say 솔직하요 — it contracts to 솔직해요.

mistakes: Saying 솔직하요 instead of 솔직해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Using 솔직하다 for 'honest' in the moral sense of not stealing or not lying (e.g. '그는 돈에 솔직해요'). For ethical honesty use 정직하다; 솔직하다 is about openly expressing real feelings.
Forgetting the discourse adverb 솔직히. To say 'honestly speaking' Koreans say 솔직히 말해서 / 솔직히 말하면, not 솔직하게 말하면 in casual speech.

examples: 반말 착해; describes a gentle heart.
A well-behaved child greets adults well.
이 식당은 양도 많은데 가격도 착해요.
This restaurant has big portions and the price is nice (cheap) too.
nuance: 착하다 is native Korean and describes an inherently good, gentle, kind-hearted, obedient nature — the goodness is a character trait, a soft and well-meaning heart, often used of children, students, and pets. The key contrast is with 친절하다: 착하다 is about who someone IS inside (good-hearted, won't hurt you, does the right thing), while 친절하다 is about considerate outward treatment in a moment; a shop clerk can be 친절한 at work while a child is 착한 by nature. Note a cultural nuance: calling an adult 착하다 can faintly imply 'naive/pushover' or sound like praising a child, so among grown-ups it is gentle but mild praise. A very common modern idiom is 가격이 착하다 / 착한 가격 ('a kind price' = pleasantly cheap, good value). It conjugates regularly (착해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'nice' in English is a catch-all (nice weather, nice food), but 착하다 applies almost only to a person's (or animal's) moral character — you cannot say 날씨가 착해요 for 'nice weather' (use 좋다), and beginners must contract 착하 + 요 to 착해요, never 착하요.

Using 착하다 as a general 'nice' for things, weather, or food (e.g. '날씨가 착해요'). 착하다 is about good-hearted character; for pleasant things use 좋다.
Praising a respected adult or boss with 착하다 expecting strong praise — it can sound like calling them a naive pushover or talking down to them. For an admirable adult, 좋은 분이에요 or 인품이 훌륭하다 is safer.

usage: to be bad for the body
examples: I'm in a bit of a bad mood.
반말 나빠; 기분이 나쁘다 = mood is bad.
Cigarettes are bad for your health.
-에 나쁘다 = 'bad for'; note 에, not 을.
I heard bad news, so my heart feels heavy.
nuance: 나쁘다 is native Korean and is the all-purpose opposite of 좋다, covering 'bad, poor, harmful, unpleasant' — bad weather, a bad mood, a bad habit, bad news, bad for your health. Near-synonyms split by domain: 나쁘다 is the broad evaluative 'bad', while 못되다 means 'wicked, ill-natured' (a morally bad, mean person, stronger and more accusatory), and 안 좋다 ('not good') is a softer, more polite way to say something is bad without the harsh punch of 나쁘다. The conjugation lesson is the ㅡ (으) drop: the stem 나쁘- loses its ㅡ before an ending starting with a vowel, and since the preceding vowel is the bright ㅏ, you add 아 → 나빠요 (past 나빴어요). Useful frame: X에 나쁘다 = 'bad for X' (몸에 나쁘다). English-speaker pitfalls: don't say 나쁘어요 — the ㅡ must drop to give 나빠요; and 'I feel bad' meaning sorry/guilty is NOT 기분이 나빠요 (that means you're in a bad/annoyed mood) — use 미안하다 for apology or 마음이 안 좋다 for feeling bad about something.

examples: The smell was off, so I didn't eat it.
오늘 그 사람 행동이 좀 이상했어요.
That person's behavior was a bit strange today.
Past 이상했어요; 행동이 이상하다 = odd behavior.
nuance: 이상하다 means 'strange, odd, weird, off' — something that doesn't seem normal or feels not-right, from a funny smell to peculiar behavior to a glitchy phone. It is Sino-Korean 異常 (이/異 'different' + 상/常 'normal, usual'), literally 'departing from the usual', which captures the feel exactly: deviating from the expected. The nearest contrast is 신기하다 (Sino 神奇), which is 'strange' in the GOOD sense of fascinating, novel, wondrous — eyes-wide curiosity — whereas 이상하다 leans negative or uneasy ('that's weird/off'); also distinguish 이상하다 from 특이하다 ('distinctive, unusual' in a more neutral, noteworthy way). It conjugates regularly (이상해요). English-speaker pitfall: English 'strange' can be admiring ('a strange and beautiful film'), but if you mean wonderfully novel use 신기하다, not 이상하다 — and saying 음식이 이상해요 implies it has gone bad or tastes wrong, a real complaint. Don't say 이상하요; it contracts to 이상해요.

examples: Today is kind of a special day.
This ring is really special to me.
Since it's a birthday, I specially prepared a cake.
nuance: 특별하다 means 'special, particular, out of the ordinary' — a day, gift, person, or place that stands apart and carries extra value or meaning. English-speaker pitfall: 'special' in English can mean 'specialized/dedicated' (a special tool, special forces), but for that meaning Korean uses the prefix 특수 (특수 장비, 특수 부대), not 특별하다; and don't say 특별하요 — it must contract to 특별해요.

structuredNuance.t: 특별하다 means 'special, particular, out of the ordinary' — a day, gift, person, or place that stands apart and carries extra value or meaning, usually precious/valued.

Watch the contrast with 특이하다 ('distinctive/peculiar'): 특별하다 = special and usually precious/valued (a special day, a special someone), while 특이하다 = unusual/peculiar in a more neutral or even slightly odd way (a peculiar habit); calling food 특이한 맛 means 'an unusual taste', not 'a wonderful taste'.
Sino-Korean 特別 (특/特 'special, particular' + 별/別 'distinguish, separate'), literally 'specially set apart'.
It conjugates regularly (특별해요). Note 특별하다 (adjective, 'is special') vs the adverb 특별히 ('specially, in particular'), which modifies verbs (특별히 신경 쓰다).

'Special' in English can mean 'specialized/dedicated' (a special tool, special forces), but for that meaning Korean uses the prefix 특수 (특수 장비, 특수 부대), not 특별하다. And don't say 특별하요 — it must contract to 특별해요.

mistakes: Saying 특별하요 instead of 특별해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Mixing up 특별하다 and 특이하다. 특별하다 = special/precious; 특이하다 = peculiar/distinctive. '특별한 냄새' (a special smell) sounds odd; for a weird-but-notable smell say 특이한 냄새.
Using 특별하다 for 'specialized/dedicated' (special equipment, special forces). That sense is 특수 (특수 장비, 특수 부대), a different word; 특별하다 is about being precious or out of the ordinary.

examples: 내일 중요한 회의가 있어서 일찍 자야 해요.
I have an important meeting tomorrow, so I should sleep early.
I value my family the most.
중요하게 생각하다 = 'to regard as important / value'.
nuance: 중요하다 means 'important, significant, crucial' — carrying weight, mattering a great deal. It is Sino-Korean 重要 (중/重 'heavy' + 요/要 'essential, vital'), a vivid literal image of 'heavy and essential', i.e. weighty and indispensable. The sharp contrast is with 필요하다 ('necessary/needed'): 중요하다 ranks how much something MATTERS in significance, while 필요하다 says something is REQUIRED to get a result — an exam can be 중요한 (it matters a lot) and a pencil 필요한 (you need it to take the test); they are not interchangeable. Also distinguish 소중하다 ('precious, dear'), which is emotional preciousness rather than functional weight. The collocation 중요하게 생각하다 / 중요하게 여기다 means 'to value, to prioritize'. It conjugates regularly (중요해요). English-speaker pitfall: learners blur 'important' and 'necessary' — for 'I need it' use 필요하다, reserving 중요하다 for 'it matters'; and never say 중요하요 (contract to 중요해요).

mistakes: Saying 중요하요 instead of 중요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 중요하다 with 필요하다. 중요하다 = matters/significant; 필요하다 = needed/required. '연필이 중요해요' (the pencil is important) usually should be '연필이 필요해요' (I need a pencil).
Using 중요하다 for emotionally precious things. For 'my family is precious to me' Koreans say 소중하다 (가족이 소중해요); 중요하다 sounds more like ranking by significance.

examples: I need your help right now.
반말 필요해; the needed thing (도움) takes 이/가.
이 일을 끝내려면 시간이 더 필요해요.
To finish this work I need more time.
There's no need to worry that much.
nuance: 필요하다 means 'to be necessary / to be needed', and it is the standard Korean way to say 'I need something'. It is Sino-Korean 必要 (필/必 'must, inevitably' + 요/要 'essential'), literally 'must-have, essential'. The grammar is the heart of the lesson and the main pitfall: Korean treats the needed thing as the GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT with 이/가, not as an object — so 'I need money' is 돈이 필요해요 (lit. 'money is necessary'), and the person who needs it is marked 한테/에게 (저한테 돈이 필요해요), never 돈을 필요해요. Contrast 필요하다 with 중요하다 ('important/matters'): needed vs. significant. The pattern -(으)ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다 means 'there is/isn't a need to ~' (걱정할 필요 없어요). It conjugates regularly (필요해요). English-speaker pitfall: because English 'need' is a transitive verb taking an object, learners wrongly say 나는 물을 필요해요; the correct, natural Korean is 나는 물이 필요해요 — and don't say 필요하요 (contract to 필요해요).

mistakes: Saying 물을 필요해요 with an object particle. 필요하다 takes the needed thing as the subject: say 물이 필요해요. Mark the needer with 한테/에게 (저한테 물이 필요해요).
Saying 필요하요 instead of 필요해요 — 하다 contracts to 해요.
Confusing 필요하다 with 중요하다. 필요하다 = required/needed to achieve something; 중요하다 = significant/matters. '시간이 중요해요' (time matters) and '시간이 필요해요' (I need time) say different things.

examples: The two of us have kind of similar personalities.
This bag is similar to that bag.
맛이 비슷해서 두 개를 자꾸 헷갈려요.
The tastes are similar, so I keep mixing the two up.
nuance: 비슷하다 means 'similar, alike, resembling' — two things that are close but not identical. It is native Korean (not a hanja word). The crucial contrast is with 같다 ('same/identical'): 비슷하다 says they RESEMBLE each other (close, comparable, but with differences), while 같다 says they are THE SAME; '가격이 비슷해요' = the prices are similar/comparable, but '가격이 같아요' = the prices are exactly the same — mixing these up changes the fact. Note the comparison particle: the thing you compare against takes 와/과 (formal) or 랑/이랑 (casual) plus 비슷하다 (A는 B와 비슷하다). Useful collocations: 성격이 비슷하다, 분위기가 비슷하다, 비슷한 또래 ('similar-aged peers'). It conjugates regularly (비슷해요). English-speaker pitfall: English says 'similar TO', so learners reach for 에/에게, but Korean uses 와/과/랑 — say 이거랑 비슷해요, not 이거에 비슷해요; and don't say 비슷하요 (contract to 비슷해요).
